title: Sharpless 112, Emission Nebula
caption: The emission nebula Sharpless 112, imaged by the Mayall 4-meter Telescope
credit: T.A. Rector (University of Alaska Anchorage) and H. Schweiker (WIYN and NOIRLab/NSF/AURA)

recognition.text: Published in the NSF NOIRLab image archive. No published rating.

story: Sharpless 112, an emission nebula in the constellation Cygnus, glows a deep red in this image. Its color comes from hydrogen gas that has been energized by a star embedded within the nebula, known as BD +45 3216.
That star is far more massive than our Sun and gives off huge quantities of ultraviolet light. The ultraviolet light is what makes the surrounding gas shine.

Ultraviolet light carries enough energy to knock electrons off hydrogen atoms. When the atoms capture electrons again, they release light at particular wavelengths, and one of the strongest of these is a deep red line called hydrogen-alpha. That is why so many emission nebulae, including this one, look red in images that include a hydrogen-alpha filter.

understand.summary: The Mosaic camera on the Mayall 4-meter Telescope used three filters. B is shown in blue, I in orange and hydrogen-alpha in red.
filters: 436 nm · Optical B (NSF Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope Mosaic I)
805 nm · Optical I (NSF Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope Mosaic I)
656 nm · Optical Ha (NSF Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope Mosaic I)
understand.eye: The hydrogen-alpha filter isolates the red glow of hydrogen, and the I filter records near-infrared light the eye cannot see.
